title: Building Your Portfolio
description: Three cheap funds, an automatic transfer, and a rule for red months.
wolfLine: Build it once. Automate it. Then leave it alone.

three-fund-portfolio.definition: A portfolio of three cheap index funds: a US stock fund, an international stock fund, and a bond fund. The split follows your timeline.
three-fund-portfolio.example: A $10,000 retirement pile with $5,000 in US stocks, $2,000 international, and $3,000 in bonds.

lessons.title: The Three Funds
lessons.summary: Home stocks, the rest of the world, and bonds.

steps.title: A complete boring mix
steps.body: A [[three-fund portfolio]] is three cheap [[index fund]]s. One holds US stocks. One holds stocks from other countries. One holds [[bond]]s. You already know each piece. The portfolio is the split, plus the [[expense ratio]]s, plus the years you leave it alone. Nothing here is a promise of a return.

steps.prompt: Which three does this lesson mean?
choices: A US stock index fund, an international stock index fund, and a bond index fund
Three individual stocks from one industry
A coin, a meme stock, and an option
steps.explain: Those three funds cover home stocks, other countries’ stocks, and bonds. The coin and the meme stock are speculation.

steps.prompt: The three-fund portfolio is three copies of the same US stock fund.
steps.explain: Two of the funds are stocks, and they are different lists: the US, and the rest of the world. The third is bonds.

steps.prompt: A $10,000 three-fund pile has $6,000 in the US stock fund and $2,000 in the international fund. How many dollars are in the bond fund?
What does the bond fund’s job stay?
steps.explain: Steadier, not magic. The emergency fund is still cash, outside this pile.

lessons.title: Three Is Enough
lessons.summary: More names often means the same stocks twice.

steps.title: Overlap
steps.body: Five US stock funds can own the same giant companies five times. That is not more [[diversification]]. It is the same bet with more [[expense ratio]]s. Three broad funds already cover the US, other countries, and bonds. Add a fund when it adds a job you do not already have.

steps.prompt: You already own a total US stock index fund. What does a second US large-company fund mostly add?
steps.explain: The big companies are already in the total market fund. The second fund repeats them.

steps.prompt: Twelve funds are always more diversified than three broad ones.
steps.explain: Diversification is different bets. Twelve overlapping funds are still one bet, with a longer fee list.

steps.prompt: Two overlapping funds each charge $15 a year. A single broad fund would charge $5. How many extra dollars a year do the two funds cost?
Owning the same companies in several funds is called ___.
steps.explain: Overlap. A new fund should add a job, not a second copy.

steps.title: Minimums, not a single correct life
steps.body: This check is a 25-year-old’s $10,000 retirement pile, decades away. Put at least $5,000 in the US stock fund, at least $2,000 in the international fund, and at least $2,000 in the bond fund. Every dollar gets assigned. A heavier stock mix would also fit this timeline. The minimums are the floor for this exercise, not a required life.

steps.prompt: Assign all $10,000. Meet each minimum.
steps.explain: The floors are $5,000, $2,000, and $2,000, which already add to $9,000. The last $1,000 can sit in any fund. The bond line in a simple fill ends at $3,000. Decades away can also hold more stocks. This is an exercise, not a personal plan.

steps.prompt: The three minimums are $5,000, $2,000, and $2,000. How many dollars is that before the last $1,000?
steps.explain: $5,000 + $2,000 + $2,000 = $9,000. The pile is $10,000, so $1,000 is still free to place.

steps.prompt: This exercise is the only legal mix for a 25-year-old.
steps.explain: The minimums keep every job on the page. More stocks would still fit a decades-long goal.

steps.prompt: Where does the emergency fund sit relative to this $10,000?
steps.explain: The emergency fund stays cash. This pile is money that can wait.

lessons.title: The Cost Check
lessons.summary: The mix is not done until you see the fee.

steps.title: Add the three fees
steps.body: Each [[fund]] has an [[expense ratio]]. On $10,000, a cheap three-fund mix in this example costs $8 a year. A similar mix of pricey funds costs $120. The jobs match. The bill does not.

steps.prompt: Which yearly fee should you walk away from?
steps.explain: $120 a year for the same kind of mix is the line to leave. The $8 mix is the cheap one.

steps.prompt: How many more dollars a year is the pricey mix?
steps.explain: $120 − $8 = $112 a year, on the same $10,000, in this example.

steps.prompt: A higher fee means the pricey mix is safer.
steps.explain: The fee is money out. Safety comes from the mix and the timeline, not from paying more.

steps.prompt: Over 10 years, if the $112 gap stayed the same, how many extra dollars would the pricey mix take?
steps.explain: 10 × $112 = $1,120. This sketch holds the fee gap still. A growing balance would make a percent fee larger.

steps.title: Take yourself out of it
steps.body: The [[three-fund portfolio]] survives if you do not have to decide every payday. The transfer happens, the buy happens, and you look again on a date you already wrote. That is the same habit as [[dollar-cost averaging]], pointed at the three funds.

steps.prompt: Put the automation in order.
items: Automatic transfer to the IRA or brokerage
Automatic buy of the three funds
Look again only on the date you wrote
steps.explain: Cash arrives, the transfer leaves, the funds get bought, and the app does not get a daily vote.

steps.prompt: Morgan can send $100 a month. How many dollars is that in a year?
steps.explain: 12 × $100 = $1,200. The mix, not the month, is the decision.

steps.prompt: An automatic plan means you never look at it again, even when the goal date changes.
steps.explain: You look on the written date, and you look when the goal itself changes. You do not look because today was red.

steps.prompt: What should the automatic buy purchase?
choices: Whatever is up the most today
The three funds in the split you chose
steps.explain: The split you already chose. The automation is not permission to chase.

lessons.title: When to Change the Plan
lessons.summary: A new date. Not a red month.

steps.title: Two pages
steps.body: One page is a 15% drop, from $10,000 to $8,500, and the goal is still 30 years away. The other page is the same kind of mix, except you now need the money in 3 years. Only the second page is a reason to change the [[asset allocation]]. The drop is the reason you wrote the rule.

docs.title: A bad month
docs.subtitle: The goal is still 30 years away
docs.note: A 15% drop. The date did not change.

docs.title: A new date
docs.subtitle: You now need the money in 3 years, not 30
docs.note: The investments did not change. The timeline did.

steps.prompt: Which page is a reason to change the mix?
steps.explain: The new date is the change. Three years cannot wear a 30-year stock mix. The 15% drop, with the date unchanged, is the moment you follow the old rule.

doc.title: A bad month
doc.subtitle: The goal is still 30 years away
doc.note: A 15% drop. The date did not change.

steps.prompt: On the bad-month page, how many dollars did the $10,000 fall?
steps.explain: $10,000 − $8,500 = $1,500. That is 15%. It is not a new goal.

steps.prompt: A 15% drop means the three-fund portfolio was the wrong idea.
steps.explain: A drop is part of owning stocks. The idea is wrong when the timeline changes, or the fees are wild, not when a year is red.

steps.prompt: You will need the money in 3 years. What should the mix do?
choices: Shift into one meme stock to catch up
Stay 100% in the riskiest fund because you are behind
steps.explain: A near date wants less swing. Catching up with a bet is how people lock in the shortfall.

lessons.title: Stay the Course
lessons.summary: The rule was written for this month.

steps.title: Do not take the meeting
steps.body: Staying the course means you keep the [[three-fund portfolio]] and the automatic buy when the screen is red, as long as the goal date is the same. Selling the $8,500 locks the $1,500 drop in. The next recovery, if it comes, happens to the people who still hold the funds. This is the habit. It is not a promise that every drop recovers on a schedule.

steps.prompt: You sell at $8,500 after the drop from $10,000. How many dollars of the drop did you lock in?
steps.explain: $10,000 − $8,500 = $1,500. The sale makes that the result.

steps.prompt: Staying the course means never changing the mix, even if you need the money next year.
steps.explain: A new date is a real change. A red month is not. The course you stay is the one that still matches the date.

steps.prompt: The goal is still 30 years away and the funds are down 15%. What is the move?
choices: Keep the funds and let the next automatic buy happen
Borrow on margin to get even faster
steps.explain: The buy happens. The rule holds. Margin is still a skip.

steps.prompt: Keeping the plan through a drop is called staying the ___.
steps.explain: The course. You set it on a calm day so a loud day cannot edit it.

lessons.title: Morgan Builds a Plan
lessons.summary: The emergency fund is done. The $100 has a job.

story.title: A hundred dollars
story.body:
Morgan’s starter emergency fund is now in place. She takes home about **$3,000** a month.

She will send **$100** a month to a Roth IRA and buy three cheap index funds: US stocks, international stocks, and bonds. She looks again on her birthday.

steps.title: Meet Morgan, later
steps.body:
Morgan is 25 and a dental assistant, the same Morgan who mapped a starter emergency fund. That cash fund is now in place. Take-home pay is still about $3,000 a month.

Morgan will send $100 a month into a Roth IRA and buy the three cheap index funds: US stocks, international stocks, and a bond fund. The look-again date is her birthday, not tomorrow morning.

steps.prompt: How many dollars a year is Morgan’s $100 a month?
steps.explain: 12 × $100 = $1,200. That is under the 2026 IRA limit of $7,500.

steps.prompt: Morgan should invest the emergency fund too, so the account looks serious.
steps.explain: The cash fund stays cash. The $100 is the investing pile.

steps.prompt: When does Morgan reread the plan?
choices: Every time a fund is red
On her birthday, unless the goal date changes
When a video names a coin
steps.explain: A written date. A red day is not a meeting.

steps.prompt: Put Morgan’s plan in order.
items: Keep the emergency fund in cash
Send $100 a month to the Roth IRA
Buy the three cheap index funds
steps.explain: Cash first, then the automatic dollars, then the three funds, then a calm date to look.

lessons.title: Portfolio Simulator
lessons.summary: Build a portfolio and fast-forward 30 years.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Building Your Portfolio
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A $9,000 portfolio is $6,000 US stocks and $2,000 international stocks. How many dollars are in bonds?
A 15% drop, with the goal still decades away, is a reason to scrap the three-fund mix.
steps.explain: The drop is why the rule exists. Change the mix when the date changes, not when the month is red.

steps.prompt: Which set is the three-fund portfolio?
choices: US stock index, international stock index, bond index
steps.explain: Home stocks, the rest of the world, and bonds. Cheap funds, then you leave them.

steps.prompt: The cheap mix costs $8 a year and the pricey mix costs $120. How many dollars a year do you keep by choosing the cheap one?
steps.explain: $120 − $8 = $112 a year in this example.
